from_feeds:
The most heavily reported development is the jihadist attack at Dioura in Mali, with France 24 Afrique carrying the story across 10 outlets and reporting the death toll at around 100 soldiers [38]. That figure is a claim from sources cited by France 24 Afrique, not an independently confirmed total. The attack is treated as a continuation, with multiple outlets describing a broader pattern of jihadist pressure on the Malian Army and its Russian partners [5][39][40][42].

On armed group activity, JNIM is named in several stories, including claims of a double attack on the Malian Army and the Russia Africa Corps [2], an attack on a camp with video of captured soldiers [40], and stepped-up operations near Bamako [31]. Islamic State Sahel is referenced through ISWAP claims of four attacks in Nigeria that killed eight [108]. The FLA appears once, in the context of JNIM expansion toward Guinea [118]. A single item describes Malian junta strikes against militant positions in the centre [44], and another says the army disrupted a terrorist network there [27].

Russian and other external actor coverage is thin. One item reports a Le Monde.fr-linked claim that the US asked Mali to constrain the Russia Africa Corps drone campaign [103], and Jeune Afrique is cited on a drone-war investigation [104]. Mali Tuareg rebels are said to have contacted the Russia Africa Corps and sought Turkish involvement [121]. Burkina Faso is reported to have rejected Western armoured vehicles and unveiled locally made equipment [52]. Benin Web TV carries a claim that Washington plans to withdraw most Reaper drones from Africa [33], and a separate item says Tehran threatened a prolonged response against US bases [17]. No other external actor activity appears in the headlines.

Political and governance coverage centres on ECOWAS and the AES bloc. ECOWAS items include a Biometric ID card push toward December use [69][98], a court conference on judgment enforcement [28], a Dakar conclave of the ECOWAS Court of Justice [18], and a report that the ECO currency launch is scheduled for 2027 [15]. AES is framed once as a French case with Russian software [49]. Niger coverage includes a military leadership change [127], nationality revocations [56][72], and a report on a reorganised high command after a coup attempt [99]. No item describes a direct AES-ECOWAS summit or a formal bloc decision.

Coverage anomalies are not clearly identifiable from the material provided. No country is reported far above or below its baseline, and the feed does not supply enough history to confirm divergence. Several items are single-source claims, including the Iran attack on a Togo-flagged tanker [48], the North Korean ballistic missile launch [29], and the Moscow drone attack [26]. There is no notable outlet divergence on any event, and the material does not support broader strategic inference.
